content: The text provided is a detailed and technical description of various survey modules and questions related to sexually transmitted infections (STIs), hepatitis B and C, HIV testing, and service uptake. 1. Reasons for Not Seeking Healthcare for STI Screening or Testing Participants are asked to provide reasons why they did not consult a healthcare provider for screening or testing for sexually transmitted infections. This question aims to identify barriers to accessing healthcare services. 2. Treatment for STIs Participants are asked whether they received treatment for the identified infections. If the response is negative or unclear, the survey skips to the end of the section. 3. Facility for STI Treatment Participants are asked about the type of facility they visited to receive treatment for sexually transmitted infections. This helps to understand the healthcare infrastructure utilized. 4. Hepatitis B and C Transmission Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is transmitted through contact with the blood, semen, or other bodily fluids of an infected person. In some countries, sexual contact is the primary mode of transmission among adults. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is primarily spread through contact with the blood of an infected person, often via contaminated needles or injecting equipment. 5. Hepatitis B and C Vaccination and Testing The survey collects information on whether participants have been vaccinated against hepatitis B, tested for hepatitis B or C, and received treatment if they tested positive. These questions are particularly relevant for people who inject drugs (PWID) and other vulnerable populations. 6. HIV Counseling and Testing HIV counseling and testing are critical components of HIV prevention and care. Ensuring individuals know their HIV status and receive appropriate prevention, care, or treatment services can significantly reduce new HIV infections. The survey measures the uptake of HIV-related services, from community outreach to antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation and retention. 7. Barriers to HIV Testing Participants who have never been tested for HIV are asked to provide reasons for not doing so. This helps identify barriers to HIV testing and service uptake. 8. HIV Testing History Participants are asked about the last time they were tested for HIV, including the year and location of the test. This information helps estimate HIV incidence and understand testing patterns. 9. HIV Diagnosis and Care Participants who tested positive for HIV are asked about their experiences with care and treatment, including whether they received antiretroviral therapy (ART) and where they first accessed these services. 10. Support Groups for People Living with HIV Participants are asked about their attendance at support groups in the past 12 months and the services or items they received from these groups. This helps assess the role of peer support in HIV care. 11. Preferred HIV Testing Locations Participants are asked where they would prefer to get tested for HIV. This question helps identify preferred service delivery points and improve accessibility. 12. Linkage to HIV Care Participants are asked whether they have registered with a healthcare provider for HIV care, including regular check-ups and access to antiretroviral medications. This question assesses the linkage to care after an HIV diagnosis. 13. Current HIV Care Participants are asked about the HIV care they are currently receiving. This includes questions about ongoing treatment and support services. 14. Survey Design Considerations The survey modules are designed to measure service uptake at the population level, including individuals who do not access services. This approach helps identify barriers to service uptake and characterize populations that are not reached by existing programs. However, small sample sizes, low prevalence rates, and poor service uptake can limit the analysis. Additionally, participants with low health literacy may find some questions challenging to answer. 15. Adaptation to Local Contexts Some questions or response options may need to be adapted to reflect local terminology and contexts. For example, terms like STD or cotrimoxazole may need to be replaced with locally recognized terms. Visual aids, such as photos of medications, can also be used to improve understanding. 16. Role of Peer Educators and Outreach Workers The survey includes questions about the role of peer educators and outreach workers in providing HIV-related information and services. Peer educators are individuals with similar risk behaviors who are trained in HIV prevention, while outreach workers are employed by organizations to deliver services in the community. 17. HIV Service Uptake Challenges Key populations, such as sex workers, men who have sex with men (MSM), transgender individuals, and PWID, may not always disclose their identities when accessing healthcare services. This makes it challenging to measure service uptake using program data. Surveys provide critical data to describe service uptake among these populations and identify barriers to care. 18. Survey Placement and Structure The module on HIV and STI services is extensive but includes a small number of core questions tailored to key populations and HIV status. Skip patterns are used to streamline the questionnaire. Depending on the survey structure, some questions may be better placed in other modules. Secondary questions should align with national guidelines or program goals. 19. HIV Testing and Counseling Services Participants are asked about their experiences with HIV testing and counseling, including the reasons for testing, the year of their last test, and the organization that conducted the test. This information helps evaluate the effectiveness of HIV testing services. 20. HIV Prevention and Vulnerability The survey explores participants' preferences for HIV testing locations and their experiences with prevention and care services. This helps identify gaps in service delivery and improve access for vulnerable populations.
